summary: Bump-in-the-Host (BIH) is a host-based IPv4-to-IPv6 translation mechanism that lets IPv4-only applications that work through NATs communicate with IPv6-only peers. It hides IPv6 by locally synthesizing IPv4 addresses. The host may be on an IPv6-only or dual-stack network.

plainLanguage.summary: An old program speaks only the old address language. A translator inside the computer pretends the new language is the old one, so the old program can talk to new-style computers.

questions: run ipv4 applications on ipv6 only network
how do ipv4 applications work on ipv6 only networks
what is a synthetic ipv4 address
subtitle: A translator inside a host that lets IPv4-only programs talk to IPv6-only servers by faking IPv4 addresses.

tldr.problem: Some IPv4-only applications still need to reach servers that are reachable only over IPv6, from hosts on IPv6-only or dual-stack networks.
tldr.mechanism: Bump-in-the-Host intercepts the application's name lookups and socket calls, hands the application a synthetic private IPv4 address mapped to the server's real IPv6 address, and translates traffic either at the socket API or at the IP layer.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6535 combines and obsoletes RFC 2767 and RFC 3338 and puts the technology on the Standards Track. The socket API variant is recommended. Using BIH together with a NAT64 is NOT RECOMMENDED.

today: RFC 6535 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 2767 and RFC 3338.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
Bump-in-the-Host (BIH) is a host-based IPv4 to IPv6 translation mechanism. It is the successor and combination of Bump-in-the-Stack (RFC 2767) and Bump-in-the-API (RFC 3338), and lets IPv4-only legacy applications talk to IPv6-only servers by synthesizing IPv4 addresses from AAAA records.

The supported applications are those that use DNS for address resolution, do not embed IP address literals in their payloads, and can do NAT traversal. The synthetic addresses come from the private pool of RFC 1918, so that NAT traversal techniques will be started. The access network can be IPv6-only or dual-stack.

The IETF recommends dual stack or tunneling for IPv6 transition and recommends against double protocol translation. Using BIH together with a NAT64 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a travel interpreter living inside your computer. The old program speaks only the old language, and the interpreter repeats everything to new-language computers.

sections.title: Two Ways to Build It
sections.content:
BIH has two implementation alternatives. As a socket API-layer translator (Bump-in-the-API), it intercepts IPv4 socket calls and invokes the matching IPv6 calls. As a network-layer translator (Bump-in-the-Stack), it intercepts IPv4 packets and converts them to IPv6 using the SIIT algorithm of RFC 6145. The socket API alternative is the recommended one.

The architecture has an Extension Name Resolver (ENR), an address mapper and, depending on the choice, either a function mapper (API layer) or a protocol translator (network layer). Where the ENR sits is independent of where translation happens.

The network-layer option can be needed when an operating system does not allow changes to its API but does allow virtual network interfaces, or the reverse. To avoid fragmentation, the host's IPv4 module SHOULD use an MTU of the IPv6 link's MTU minus 20 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The interpreter can sit at the door where programs make requests, or further down where messages are already packaged. The first spot is the better one.

sections.title: Name Resolution and the ENR
sections.content:
The ENR answers the application's name lookup. In the API-layer version, a call like gethostbyname() is redirected to getaddrinfo(), which resolves both A and AAAA records and works with any name resolution technique the system uses. In the network-layer version, the ENR sends an extra AAAA query alongside the A query and then returns the real A reply or synthesizes a new one.

If an A reply contains non-excluded real IPv4 addresses, the ENR MUST NOT synthesize addresses. It asks the address mapper for a synthetic IPv4 address for each IPv6 address when the A query gets a negative response, all received IPv4 addresses were excluded, or the A query timed out. By default it SHOULD exclude addresses that should not appear in DNS or on the wire.

Reverse lookups for a synthetic address MUST be turned into a reverse lookup of the real IPv6 address, while other reverse lookups pass through unmodified. DNS cache entries for synthetic addresses MUST be flushed when BIH shuts down or mapping entries are cleared. Network-layer synthesis can break DNSSEC validation, so the host's main resolver SHOULD NOT validate A records while BIH runs; the API-layer approach avoids this and is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: When the old program asks where a website lives and only a new-style address exists, the helper makes up an old-style address and writes down which real address it stands for.

sections.title: The Address Mapper and Address Pools
sections.content:
The address mapper keeps a pool of RFC 1918 IPv4 addresses and a table of pairs: a synthetic IPv4 address and the destination's real IPv6 address. It assigns a new entry when the ENR gets only IPv6 addresses, when the only real IPv4 addresses are excluded ones such as 127.0.0.1, or when the function mapper sees an IPv6 packet from a source without an entry.

RFC 1918 space was chosen because legacy applications understand it as private. The ranges 127/8 and 169.254/16 were rejected because of assumptions applications may make. Mapping entries should live a long time, since an application may reuse an address much longer than the DNS time to live, and address-pool granularity can be per node, per user or per process. The RFC recommends these pools:

  • Primary source addresses: 172.21.112.0/20; secondary: 10.170.224.0/20.
  • Primary destination addresses: 10.170.160.0/20; secondary: 172.21.80.0/20.

Source and destination ranges are on different subnets so applications make no on-link assumptions and enable NAT traversal. A small chance remains that a synthesized destination conflicts with a real attached IPv4 network.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper keeps a notebook of pretend addresses and the real ones they stand for, picking pretend ones from a set that old programs know are private.

sections.title: How Traffic Flows
sections.content:
In Scenario 1 an IPv4-only application on a host in the IPv6-only Internet talks to an IPv6-only server. In Scenario 2 the host is on a dual-stack network, but the server sits on a private IPv4 site with public IPv6 addresses, so IPv6 is the only way to reach it.

With the API-layer version, the application resolves a name, receives a synthetic IPv4 address, then calls IPv4 socket functions. The translator looks up the real IPv6 address, performs the matching IPv6 socket action, and maps replies back to IPv4. ICMPv4 and ICMPv6 messages MUST be translated as defined by SIIT.

Other rules matter too. If the host has any IPv4 interface available, BIH MUST NOT translate IPv4 to IPv6 for dual-stack destinations. If an IPv4 interface comes up mid-run, BIH MUST stop starting new translated sessions and MAY disconnect active ones. An explicitly bound socket MUST NOT be changed. Multicast translation is not supported, and no Application-Level Gateway is specified.
sections.plainLanguage: The program calls a pretend address, the helper swaps it for the real one, sends the message and swaps the answer back before the program sees it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
These considerations follow, but not completely, those of NAT64 (RFC 6146) and DNS64 (RFC 6147). Any protocol that protects IP header information is essentially incompatible with BIH: end-to-end IPsec verification fails with AH and with ESP in transport mode. UDP encapsulation (RFC 3948) can restore it, but the extensions are out of scope.

BIH MUST offer Endpoint-Independent Mapping and MAY offer Address-Dependent Mapping. Security properties come from filtering, not address mapping.

BIH can be a denial-of-service victim. An attacker can exhaust the synthetic address pool by causing DNS queries that make the ENR synthesize A records, or exhaust memory with fragments, so implementations MUST protect against this, for example by limiting fragment storage. BIH modifies DNS answers, which DNSSEC treats as bogus, so it can interfere with DNSSEC.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the helper rewrites messages, some safety seals break. A mischievous visitor could also use up all the pretend addresses, so the helper must keep limits.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2767 and RFC 3338
sections.content:
RFC 6535 combines and obsoletes both earlier documents. RFC 2767 was Informational and RFC 3338 was Experimental; the IETF decided this technology should be on the Standards Track.

  • RFC 3338 used unassigned addresses such as 0.0.0.1 to 0.0.0.255, which should not have been used. RFC 1918 addresses replace them.
  • Reverse (PTR) lookups are now supported, which neither earlier RFC covered.
  • DNSSEC considerations are added, which RFC 2767 lacked.
  • The socket API-layer option is recommended over network-layer translation, favoring the RFC 2767 approach over the one of RFC 3338.
  • Lesser changes include address exclusion sets, host DNS cache handling, updated examples and security text.
sections.plainLanguage: Two older recipes were merged into one better recipe, with safer pretend addresses and a clear favorite way to cook it.
